t: Why Kindness Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy agement-strategy/
q: You see, students are accustomed to having anger and frustration attached to accountability. They’re used to teachers enforcing consequences with an air of revenge or reciprocity.
Which encourages them to deny responsibility for their misbehavior. It encourages them to argue and point the finger elsewhere.
If, however, they receive a consequence from someone they like and respect, and it’s given impersonally , then the response is quite different.
They’ll accept and even agree with your consequence. They’ll take responsibility, naturally and without you having to say another word.
Your steady, day-after-day consistency , in both personality and commitment to accountability, has a transformational effect on students.
It proves to them that when you enforce a consequence, it’s done purely, and from a caring heart. It proves to them that you’re a leader worth following.

t: How To Have A Nicer, Friendlier Class
q: Teachers tend to respond in one of two ways. Either they get angry and demand civility through lectures, threats, talking-tos, and how-dare-yous. Or they overwhelm their students with kindness.
The first will cause your students to dislike you. It will cause behind-the-back rebelliousness and resentment. It will bring tension into your classroom and cause more incivility, not less.
The problem with the second approach is that your students won’t respect you. They’ll view you as a pushover. You’ll be brushed aside, if not run over.
To improve the civility in your classroom, you must combine a kind, easygoing disposition with a faithful and unwavering commitment to accountability.
This sends the message that while rudeness and disrespect toward you or their fellow classmates won’t be tolerated, even a sliver, it isn’t personal.
x: Demanding civility through lectures and threats alone tends to increase resentment and behind-the-back rebellion.
Both approaches fail, he argues — the first breeds resentment and rebellion, while the second causes students to lose respect and view the teacher as a pushover.
Both approaches fail, he argues — the first breeds resentment and rebellion, while the second causes students to lose respect and view the teacher as a pushover.
His proposed solution is to combine both qualities simultaneously: a kind, easygoing disposition paired with faithful, unwavering accountability.
This combination communicates that disrespect won't be tolerated, but that consequences are never personal, and that forgiveness is always extended the next day.

t: Is It Ever Okay For Students To Leave Their Seat Without Permission? eat-without-permission/
q: The solution is to define for your students precisely and narrowly what is and isn’t okay and when it is and isn’t okay to do it.
You would then model what getting a tissue looks like—which would include taking a direct route to and from the tissue box without interrupting others.
Explicit modeling lays it all out, puts it on record, and removes any excuse to be up and out of their seats for any other reason or in any other way.
Finally, it’s important that you detail any time or times you don’t want them to be able to get up, like while you’re giving directions or providing instruction, for example.
Narrow definitions and precise modeling are the keys to successfully allowing reasonable exceptions to your rules.
As long as you hold accountable any student who strays even a nanometer from your narrow exceptions, you’ll have a more focused and peaceful classroom.
x: His solution is precision: define narrowly and explicitly which actions are exceptions to the raise-your-hand rule, and model exactly what performing them correctly — and incorrectly — looks like, including the specific…

His solution is precision: define narrowly and explicitly which actions are exceptions to the raise-your-hand rule, and model exactly what performing them correctly — and incorrectly — looks like, including the specific…
Explicit modeling of both correct and incorrect ways to perform an exception removes ambiguity and excuses.
Teachers should also specify times when even approved exceptions are off-limits, such as during direct instruction.
Linsin argues that narrow definitions paired with precise modeling remove any excuse for wandering or arguing, since expectations are on record and non-negotiable.

He recommends limiting exceptions to just three or four commonly requested needs, spending about thirty minutes teaching and modeling them, and then holding students strictly accountable for any deviation.
